movement_source: row 'Net profit after tax from continuing operations – cash basis', column Full Year Ended 30 Jun 25 (cash basis) $M -> column Full Year Ended 30 Jun 26 (cash basis) $M
headline: CBA's cash NPAT from continuing operations rose $730m or 7% to $10,982m in FY26 from $10,252m in FY25 (ev-8, ev-12, ev-50). The bank leads with total operating income of $30,224m, up 6% (+6.2%) from $28,465m (ev-1, ev-29), and operating performance (pre-provision profit) of $16,469m, up 6% (+6.5%) from $15,469m (ev-5, ev-31). Statutory NPAT was $10,866m against cash NPAT of $10,982m for FY26; statutory NPAT rose $750m or 7% including discontinued operations, and $778m or 8% on a continuing-operations basis to $10,911m (ev-10, ev-13, ev-48) — a faster statutory growth rate than cash, because the non-cash reconciliation items differ between years: loss on acquisition/disposal/closure of businesses of $(62)m in FY26 versus $(190)m in FY25, and hedging and IFRS volatility of $(54)m versus $+53m (ev-23, ev-24). CBA attributes the result to "lending volume growth in our core businesses, with underlying net interest margin broadly stable", partly offset by higher expenses from inflation and technology investment and a higher loan impairment expense (ev-47).

drivers.narrative: NII $25,586m, "an increase of $1,563 million or 7%", driven by a $92bn or 8% AIEA rise to $1,246bn, partly offset by NIM down 3bpts to 2.05%. Average lending IEA +$60bn or 7%: home loans +$32bn or 5% to $630bn, business/corporate +$27bn or 10% to $299bn across diversified Business Banking industries plus institutional and structured lending. Excluding liquid assets, NIM was stable.

Volume is the stated primary cause of the NII gain but CBA does not split it into dollars. AIEA rose $92bn or 8% to $1,246bn; average lending IEA +$60bn or 7%. Presentation average volume growth: home loans 5%, business loans 10%, institutional loans 11%, deposits 8%. Liquid assets +$15bn or 9% and institutional repos +$11bn, which CBA says have "broadly neutral impacts on net interest income".

NIM fell 3bpts from 2.08% to 2.05%. The results book's own walk: Liquids (3)bpts, Asset pricing (5)bpts, Funding costs flat, Portfolio mix +2bpts, Basis risk flat, Capital/Replicating and Other +5bpts, Treasury & Markets (2)bpts. Asset pricing reflects home lending pricing down 4bpts and business/institutional lending down 1bpt on competition; mix reflects favourable asset mix from business lending growth and funding mix from deposit growth. Unit is bps, not $m.

Other operating income $4,638m, "an increase of $196 million or 4%". Sub-parts: commissions +$135m or 6% to $2,234m on higher insurance income including a CommInsure General Insurance sale milestone payment, higher volume-driven equities income and syndication fees, offset by lower deposit fees from fee waivers, lower credit card fees from higher loyalty costs and lower FX; other income +$46m or 42% to $156m on minority investments and a Gemini IPO fair value gain, offset by lower Structured Asset Finance revenue after the aircraft lease portfolio sale; lending fees +$12m; funds management +$12m; trading income (9)m.

UNDERLYING (ex restructuring and notable items) expenses rose from $12,866m to $13,585m, +6% (+5.6%), a negative $719m contribution. CBA's own walk: Inflation +$455m, Investment in technology +$444m, Investment in frontline and operations +$128m, Other +$96m, Productivity (404)m. Reasons: wage inflation including higher super guarantee, vendor IT inflation +5%, higher cloud consumption and software licensing, and investment in infrastructure, resilience and AI. Cumulative cost savings $2,472m FY26 vs $2,068m FY25. Underlying cost-to-income improved 30bpts, 45.2% to 44.9%.

Notable items rose from $(130)m to $(170)m, +31%, a $40m adverse delta on top of underlying expenses. FY26 comprises provisions for the settlement of legal proceedings in NZ, an additional goodwill payment to certain customers from ASIC's Better Banking review, and domestic customer remediation; FY25 was domestic and NZ customer remediation plus a Bankwest restructuring provision. Including these, headline operating expenses grew 5.8% to $13,755m from $12,996m.

LIE $788m, "an increase of $62 million or 9%" from $726m — a negative contribution. CBA cites higher collective provisions mainly reflecting portfolio growth, increased geopolitical risk and macroeconomic uncertainty. By division: Retail Banking Services +$106m to $378m on geopolitical risk, macroeconomic uncertainty and cost-of-living pressures; New Zealand +$11m to $66m; partly offset by Business Banking (45)m to $310m on lower individually assessed charges and write-backs, and IB&M (16)m to $33m on release of individually assessed provisions. Home loan 90+ arrears 0.73%.

Corporate tax expense rose from $(4,491)m to $(4,699)m, +5%, a negative $208m contribution to cash earnings. The tax expense grew more slowly than the 6% rise in net profit before tax ($15,681m vs $14,743m), consistent with the FY26 effective tax rate of 30.0% disclosed in the presentation. The delta is my own subtraction of the two full-year columns, not a movement CBA states in dollars.

notable_items: FY26 restructuring and notable items of $170m: provisions for the settlement of legal proceedings in NZ; an additional goodwill payment to certain customers from ASIC's Better Banking review; domestic customer remediation (ev-3, ev-11)
FY25 comparative notable items of $130m: domestic and NZ customer remediation plus a Bankwest restructuring provision (ev-3, ev-11)

Within other operating income (inside the cash result, not a reconciliation item): a milestone payment on the sale of CommInsure General Insurance and a fair value gain on the Gemini investment following its IPO (ev-19, ev-61, ev-64)

Statutory-to-cash reconciliation items, NOT bridge drivers: loss on acquisition/disposal/closure of businesses $(62)m FY26 vs $(190)m FY25; hedging and IFRS volatility $(54)m FY26 vs $+53m FY25 (ev-23, ev-24)

disagreements.topic: Cash vs statutory NPAT growth rate
disagreements.explanation: Statutory grew faster because the non-cash reconciliation items were less adverse in FY26 in aggregate on disposals ($(62)m vs $(190)m) though hedging/IFRS volatility swung negative ($(54)m vs $+53m). These explain the statutory-cash gap within each year, not the year-on-year cash movement, so they are excluded from the bridge. Cash NPAT is CBA's core measure (ev-8, ev-13, ev-23, ev-24).

The profit announcement prints 6% in its change column and also states the $719m increase; the presentation prints the unrounded +5.6% for underlying and +5.8% for headline. The dollar movement of $719m is identical on both (ev-2, ev-30, ev-38).

disagreements.topic: FY25 Retail Banking Services cash NPAT comparative
disagreements.explanation: The FY26 profit announcement footnotes that comparative information has been restated to conform with current-period presentation; divisional FY25 comparatives shifted (RBS $5,395m to $5,330m, IB&M $1,224m to $1,238m, NZ $1,198m to $1,195m). Group FY25 cash NPAT of $10,252m is unchanged, so the movement is unaffected (ev-26, ev-50).

limitations: CBA does not publish a single cash-NPAT waterfall for FY26 vs FY25. I built the bridge from the results book's Group Performance Summary component columns (ev-1 to ev-8), corroborated by two PRIMARY walks (operating income FY25->FY26 and underlying operating expenses FY25->FY26) whose sum checks passed. The components reconcile exactly: +1,563 NII +196 OOI -719 underlying opex -40 notables -62 LIE -208 tax = +730, so residual is zero. The additivity framing is mine, not a published CBA bridge.

The tax contribution of -$208m is my own subtraction of the FY26 and FY25 corporate tax expense columns, not a movement CBA states in dollars; confidence capped at 78 accordingly. I did not read the tax note (page 35) that would explain the effective tax rate fall from 30.5% to 30.0%, so the reason behind the tax movement rests only on the rate figure printed in the presentation summary rather than on CBA's own tax commentary.

NII is NOT split into volume and margin dollars by CBA. The margin driver is quantified only in bps (-3bpts, walk ev-66) and the volume driver only in balance-sheet dollars ($92bn AIEA, $60bn lending). Neither can be converted to a $m earnings contribution from the evidence, so nii.volume carries no contribution and nii.margin carries a bps unit that must not be added into the $m bridge — nii at +$1,563m is the additive component.

QUALIFICATION CBA ITSELF MAKES that changes what the NIM fall means: the largest single negative in the margin walk, liquids and repos (-3bpts in the results book walk, -4bpts in the slide walk), is explicitly labelled "Minimal impact on earnings" and "broadly neutral impact on net interest income", because the $15bn liquid-asset and $11bn repo growth carries matching funding. Excluding liquids, CBA says NIM was STABLE. So the headline 3bpt NIM decline overstates the earnings drag, and the true margin story is competition (-5bpts asset pricing) offset by hedge earnings (+5bpts capital/replicating).

The two NIM walks differ in framing: the results book prints seven bars (Liquids -3, Asset pricing -5, Funding costs 0, Portfolio mix +2, Basis risk 0, Capital/Replicating and Other +5, Treasury & Markets -2) while the slide prints six (Liquids & repos -4, Asset pricing -5, Funding costs 0, Portfolio mix +2, Interest rate risk hedging +5, Treasury & Markets -1). I adopted the results book walk per source hierarchy and did not mix bars across the two.

The expense walk's "Other" bar of +$96m is not explained by any narrative I read, and the composition of the +$455m inflation and +$444m technology bars against the income-statement category movements (staff +$288m, IT services +$393m, occupancy -$19m, other +$57m) is a different cut that CBA does not reconcile to the walk.

Corroboration is adequate but uneven: the movement, operating income, pre-provision profit and cash/statutory NPAT are confirmed across the profit announcement, the presentation and the ASX announcement, and FY25 comparatives were checked against the FY25 profit announcement. The notable-items delta (-$40m) and the tax delta (-$208m) appear in only the profit announcement columns, so those two sit at or below 85.

I did not read the FY26 divisional pages in full, so the attribution is Group-level. Divisional cash NPAT levels are cited (RBS $5,587m vs $5,330m, Business Banking $4,544m vs $4,092m +11%) but I have not verified the drivers behind each division's contribution.
Research stopped early: the tool-call budget (40 calls) was reached, so the evidence behind this answer is less complete than a full run's.
Expenses are claimed on the underlying/notable split; the bank equally publishes the combined headline framing, so both claims are capped at 80.

Cash net profit after tax (cash NPAT or cash profit) from continuing operations increased $730 million or 7% on the prior year to $10,982 million. The result was driven by a 6% increase in operating income and a 6% increase in operating expenses 2, as well as a $62 million increase in loan impairment expense.

numbers.label: Cash NPAT increase FY26 vs FY25

evidence_records.quote: The Bank’s statutory net profit after tax (NPAT) from continuing operations for the full year ended 30 June 2026 increased $778 million or 8% on the prior year to $10,911 million. The Bank’s statutory NPAT (including discontinued operations) increased $750 million or 7% on the prior year to $10,866 million.

Net interest income increased 7%, primarily driven by an 8% or $92 billion increase in Average Interest Earning Assets (AIEA). Excluding the impact of liquid assets, underlying Net Interest Margin (NIM) was stable. Average lending interest earning assets increased by $60 billion or 7% due to growth in home, business and institutional lending.

Underlying NIM was supported by higher earnings on replicating portfolio and capital hedges, and favourable portfolio mix, offset by the impact of increased lending price competition and Treasury and Markets.

Other operating income increased 4% primarily driven by higher insurance income and the benefit of one-off gains 3, higher volume driven equities income, partly offset by lower Structured Asset Finance revenue following the sale of the aircraft lease portfolio, lower foreign exchange income, lower deposit fees due to fee waivers and lower credit card fees from higher loyalty costs.

Operating expenses 2 increased 6% mainly driven by inflation, and investment in technology to support infrastructure, resilience and AI capabilities, as well as higher cloud computing volumes and software licensing, and higher staff costs in frontline and operations, partly offset by productivity initiatives and favourable FX.

Loan impairment expense (LIE) increased $62 million, with higher collective provisions mainly reflecting portfolio growth, increased geopolitical risk and macroeconomic uncertainty. Home loan 90+ day arrears were 0.73%, an increase of 10 basis points on the prior half,
